node.label: Saidiya Hartman
node.description: Scholar of African American literature and cultural history who makes slavery’s afterlives and the conditions of historical narration central problems. Her 2008 essay joins critical fabulation to restraint and the acknowledgment of unrecoverable lives. In her own account of Wayward Lives, ordinary young Black women are social thinkers and experimenters, rather than pathological cases in state records. Respect and criticism coexist in her reading of Du Bois: she values his intellectual achievement while questioning the Philadelphia survey’s class and gender judgments.

node.scope_note: Read on 24 October 2026: “Venus in Two Acts,” pp.7–14, in a public institutional copy; the Jean interview in full; selected Bulley interview answers on archives, Lose Your Mother and waywardness. The three books remain unread beyond these descriptions and retrospective accounts. Acknowledged narrative failure and limits of speculation are part of the method. The Du Bois critique is her 2020 statement, not an independently read book passage. Existing roster notes and their earlier unread qualifications remain as historical reading records; the new sources state this later scope. Existing edges_1213 and _1215 retain the aggregate archive/Atlantic and archive/Black-history interpretations.

verification.note: Crossref only (1 June 2008, pp. 1–14); Duke's journal platform returned 403 and Project MUSE a challenge page; unread. Copies on course sites were not opened. Addendum 2026-10-28: Fresh complete 1–14 article read in actual 15-leaf McGill-hosted published PDF including wrapper, https://www.mcgill.ca/english/files/english/hartman_venus_in_two_acts.pdf . Printed 10/n32 visually checked. Hartman cites Trouillot alongside Stephan Palmié precisely while asking whether obeying the historical guild consigned captive girls to oblivion. The manufactured-certainties quotation is Palmié, not Trouillot; n33 archive formulation is Foucault, not an automatic Trouillot quotation. Critical fabulation 11–12 retains narrative restraint, impossibility and own acknowledged failure; citation does not make Trouillot sole origin of method. Her 1997 cited manifestation distinct from original 1995/anniversary 2015. Other named resources in full article belong to Hartman, not automatically Trouillot.
